evidence_quotes.quote: This paper investigates the impact of water service privatization in Bolivia.
Source: Authors’ calculations based on Encuesta Nacional de Empleo (1996), from the Instituto Nacional de Estadı´stica (INE) de Bolivia.
Notes: Marginal values reported. Since each of the cities is either classiﬁed as “privatized” or “not-privatized”
However, the concessionaire failed to meet the targets stipulated in the contract.
for new connections in El Alto and did not suﬀer any penalties

country.comment: Empirical household survey and institutional analysis focuses on Bolivia's four largest cities: La Paz, El Alto, Santa Cruz de la Sierra, and Cochabamba (Table 1 briefly lists background examples of cancelled concessions in Argentina, Bolivia, and Uruguay).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Summary, and Section 1; PDF p. 3, Section 3 & Table 2

effect_estimate.comment: Note that in the extracted PDF text layer, several minus signs in tables rendered as spaces (e.g., Cochabamba QI coverage fell from 63.3% in 1996 to 25.9% in 2005, a -37.4 percentage-point change, and El Alto's 2001 concentration index is stated in the text on p. 2570 as negative -0.018). The positive long-run DID marginal effect (+0.077*** and +0.075***) is confirmed in both Section 6 text and Table 12.
effect_estimate.value: In difference-in-differences (DID) probit regressions comparing privatized cities (La Paz and El Alto) with non-privatized cities (Santa Cruz and Cochabamba), privatization had no statistically significant short-run marginal effect on household in-house piped water access over 1996–2001 (Effect = 0.025, SE = 0.025, N = 3,240 controlling for log per capita income; Effect = 0.025, SE = 0.025, N = 3,277 controlling for dwelling characteristics), but had a significant positive long-run marginal effect over 1996–2005 (Effect = 0.077, SE = 0.016, p < 0.01, N = 2,917 with income control; Effect = 0.075, SE = 0.015, p < 0.01, N = 2,945 with dwelling controls). Descriptively (1996–2005), piped water coverage rose in La Paz from 87.9% to 96.6% (poorest quintile QI: 83.4% to 96.2%, +12.8 percentage points, p < 0.05) and in El Alto from 76.2% to 87.8% (QI: 55.6% to 86.0%, +30.3 percentage points, p < 0.05), stayed flat in cooperative-run Santa Cruz (95.5% to 95.6%; QI: 90.2% to 90.1%), and fell in public-run Cochabamba from 76.5% to 61.8% (QI: 63.3% to 25.9%, -37.4 percentage points, p < 0.05). Water access concentration indices declined in La Paz (0.044 to 0.010) and El Alto (0.077 to 0.011). However, an independent 2005 regulatory audit (SISAB) found the concessionaire installed only 46,438 of the contractually mandated 71,752 new water connections in El Alto by 2001 (64.7% of target) without incurring penalties; tariffs rose 12% in 2001 (indexed to USD) and water connection fees rose from US$155 to US$196 (sewerage US$180 to US$249). Non-affordability (>3% of income among connected QI households, 2001–2005) rose in La Paz from 34.8% to 42.1%, fell in El Alto from 25.6% to 15.1% (while mean QI income share spent on water rose from 1.9% to 2.6%), and remained highest in Santa Cruz (78.4% to 73.1%), culminating in public protests and contract termination/renationalization in 2005–2006.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section 2; PDF pp. 6–12, Sections 5–7 & Tables 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, and 12

mechanism_certainty.comment: Although appraised with ROBINS-I as a DID policy evaluation, overall risk of bias is Serious (only 2 treated vs. 2 non-randomly selected comparison cities, diverging 1992–1996 pre-trends, Cochabamba's own 1999–2000 privatization/water-war shock and sharp coverage drop in the comparator group, changing survey water-access item wording across waves in Table 4, small 2001 El Alto sample of n = 56, unclustered standard errors, and the authors' explicit caution on p. 2568 against causal inference), which caps certainty at 2 under CODEBOOK.md §9. Rating 2 is warranted because the paper directly documents the institutional/contractual mechanisms (concession connection mandates, elimination of standpipes, USD-indexed tariff and connection-fee increases, SISAB regulatory audit findings of 64.7% target completion, non-enforcement of contractual penalties, and expanded billing/metering) alongside empirical household data.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section 2; PDF p. 5, Section 4; PDF pp. 10–12, Sections 5(c), 6, and 7

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines concession contract design and subsystem/neighborhood expansion planning mandates plus elimination of communal standpipes in favor of mandatory in-house network connections (ELIGIBILITY: planning, service_area); block tariffs, USD tariff indexation, fixed billing fees, and connection fee increases (BURDEN: fees); connection-fee financing plans and self-build labor/materials options vs. subsidy bans (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: accommodation); regulatory monitoring/auditing by SISAB, non-enforcement of contractual penalties for missed connection targets, consumer complaints, and early contract termination (ENFORCEMENT: sanction, complaint); and closed-door contract negotiations, cooperative governance boards, and public protests/mobilization (participation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, planning, service_area, fees, accommodation, complaint, sanction, participation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2–3, Section 2; PDF p. 5, Section 3(c); PDF pp. 10–12, Sections 5(c) and 7

outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 3–5, Section 3 & Table 4; PDF pp. 6–11, Sections 5–6 & Tables 5–12

publication_year.comment: Published in World Development, Vol. 40, No. 12, pp. 2564–2577, 2012 (final revision accepted May 25, 2012).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, journal footer and copyright line

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary causal-inference component is a non-randomized quasi-experimental difference-in-differences (DID) probit evaluation comparing cities that experienced a policy shock (water utility privatization in La Paz and El Alto) against comparator cities without sustained privatization (Santa Cruz and Cochabamba) using pre-reform (1996) and post-reform (2001, 2005) repeated cross-sectional household surveys. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the design-matched tool for DID studies.

sample_size.comment: Table 2 reports unweighted household sample sizes across four official INE surveys in the four studied cities (La Paz, El Alto, Cochabamba, Santa Cruz), summing to 7,311 households across 1992–2005. Table 12 reports exact analytic sample sizes (and weighted population sizes of 1,385,919 to 1,487,615) for the pairwise 1996–2001 and 1996–2005 DID probit models.

study_design.comment: Combines a repeated cross-sectional difference-in-differences (DID) probit regression with descriptive statistical analyses (Welch t-tests, Kakwani achievement index counterfactuals, concentration indices/curves, and expenditure-based affordability metrics) and institutional case analysis of concession governance and renationalization.
study_design.value: Quasi-experimental difference-in-differences (DID) probit regression and distributional/affordability analysis using repeated cross-sectional household surveys (1992, 1996, 2001, 2005) across four cities comparing privatized (La Paz, El Alto) versus cooperative (Santa Cruz) and public (Cochabamba) water provision, paired with institutional analysis of concession contracts
